title: Polarized neutron scattering as a probe for vortex-type spin correlations in iron oxide multicore assemblies
authors: Venus Rai, Ivan Titov, Elizabeth M. Jefremovas, Štefan Liščák, Sivarenjini Shan, Nina-Juliane Steinke, Jonathan Leliaert, Álvaro Gallo-Córdova, María P. Morales, Davide Peddis, Pierfrancesco Maltoni, Luis Fernández Barquín, Andreas Michels, Michael P. Adams
abstract: We report an experimental investigation of the magnetic microstructure of iron oxide multicore assemblies by means of polarized small-angle neutron scattering (SANS). Guided by a recently developed analytical theory for vortex-state magnetic nanoparticles, we provide a quantitative comparison between the measured and calculated cross sections, revealing signatures that are consistent with vortex-type magnetization configurations at low applied magnetic fields. In particular, the field evolution and the characteristic isotropic ring-type feature of the spin-flip scattering intensity at intermediate momentum transfers are in line with the formation of flux-closure states. The latter are stabilized by the interplay of exchange, Zeeman, and magnetostatic energies. The methodology allows for a statistically significant characterization of vortex states in densely packed nanoparticle systems, thereby complementing surface-sensitive techniques that are commonly limited to the observation of spin structures in individual particles.
summary: This work uses polarized small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) to experimentally map the magnetic microstructure of iron oxide nanoflowers. By analyzing the spin-flip scattering intensity at low applied fields, the researchers provide strong evidence for the formation of vortex-type magnetization states within these assemblies. This methodology demonstrates SANS's power in characterizing complex, non-uniform magnetic correlations in densely packed nanomaterials.
main_problem: The study investigates vortex-type spin correlations within iron oxide multicore assemblies.
main_result: Experimental measurements of the spin-flip SANS cross section reveal an isotropic ring structure at low fields, which is quantitatively consistent with theoretical predictions for flux-closure states stabilized by magnetostatic and exchange energies.
method: Polarized small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) was employed to probe the magnetic microstructure of the assemblies.
model_or_system: The physical system consists of iron oxide nanoflowers, modeled using a linear vortex magnetization Ansatz. The analysis compares measured spin-flip cross sections against theoretical models incorporating particle interactions via structure factors.
key_observables: Spin-flip SANS cross section (dSigma_sf/dOmega) and its field evolution at intermediate momentum transfers (q).
important_parameters: Low applied magnetic fields are crucial for observing vortex formation; the characteristic isotropic ring feature is key.
main_assumptions: The analysis uses an effective model incorporating the Percus-Yevick structure factor to account for dense packing and size distribution, building upon initial dilute ensemble approximations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows TEM images of nanoflowers and magnetization hysteresis. Figure 2 compares experimental spin-flip scattering at different fields (1.0 T vs 0.01 T) with the linear vortex model prediction.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical system and theoretical framework for vortex modeling to presenting quantitative comparisons between measured SANS data and calculated cross sections, culminating in evidence supporting the vortex state formation.
why_interesting: While focused on magnetism, the use of scattering techniques to probe mesoscopic, non-uniform magnetic order parameters (like vortices) provides an analogy for studying complex, spatially varying order parameters in other condensed matter systems.
